facts.claim: "Angel" was released 22 June 2022 as First Aid Kit's first new original music in about three years, and it was later included on the album Palomino.
The song is credited to Klara Söderberg, Johanna Söderberg and Daniel Bengtson as writers.
Daniel Bengtson produced Palomino, the album that includes "Angel". The duo recorded it at his Studio Rymden in Stockholm.

Palomino was the duo's first record made in Sweden since their 2010 debut The Big Black & the Blue. Credits list Kyle Jeffrey Crane on drums and percussion, and Daniel Bengtson on production, guitar, bass and backing vocals.

The duo said the song was written in the wake of major global events over the previous few years. They called it a hopeful tune about accepting other people even when you don't see eye to eye, and about being kinder to yourself.
The duo said they wanted the song to feel really big but vulnerable, something you can cry to and dance to.

Klara Söderberg said she was scared of the lyrics, which she thought were too direct and a little cheesy. She was reluctant to put the first studio version on the record, but she came around after Daniel Bengtson added an acoustic guitar part that reminded her of The Mamas & The Papas.
Klara said a trans woman they met in Halifax the day after release told them the song was about her life.
Johanna said "Out Of My Head" was meant to be the first single, but the label wanted another song released first, which was "Angel".
The video for "Angel" was directed by longtime collaborator Mats Udd. Palomino was announced the same day as the single, and the duo called it probably their most pop-sounding record yet.

research.lineage: First Aid Kit are a Swedish sister duo usually described as folk or alt-country, known for sibling harmonies. With "Angel" and Palomino they moved toward a more pop-leaning sound.

draft:
The hardest line in **Angel** isn't the shout. It's the quiet bit of logic in the second verse: "But if I didn't speak it, it wouldn't be real." Anyone who has sat on a feeling for years knows that bargain. Keep the pain unsaid and you can pretend it's manageable. First Aid Kit's song is about breaking that deal, and about how exposed it feels to do it.

Klara Söderberg has said she was scared of these lyrics and worried they were too direct and a little cheesy. That fear is also the song's subject. The opening lines describe a whole life spent afraid and name anxiety, shame and doubt in one flat list. Then the narrator admits to wanting to let it all out at the top of their lungs. Wanting, not doing. The shout stays a wish. The chorus asks for love, compassion and passion, and it slips self-forgiveness into the middle of that list, the one thing nobody else can actually hand over. It gets asked for anyway, which is how it goes when you can't yet give it to yourself.

The real turn comes when the chorus repeats with one word changed, "don't" becoming "can't": "I love you even if you can't love me." Don't is a refusal. Can't is a limit. The second version forgives someone for what they aren't able to give, and it's hard not to hear the narrator offering the same grace inward. The sisters wrote it in the wake of major world events, and they called it a hopeful song about accepting people you don't see eye to eye with and being kinder to yourself. The lyric folds both into one gesture.

Klara nearly kept the first studio version off the record. She changed her mind after producer and co-writer Daniel Bengtson added an acoustic guitar part that reminded her of The Mamas & The Papas. That strummed folk-pop brightness carries everything, along with a walking bass line and a plain kick-snare-hi-hat beat at a relaxed, moderate tempo. The two voices are clear and bright. Sometimes they lock in unison, and sometimes one climbs above the melody. It's clean and polished, full without crowding. The duo made it at Bengtson's Studio Rymden in Stockholm for Palomino, which they called probably their most pop-sounding record yet, and they wanted something big but vulnerable, a song you could cry to and dance to.

The last verse brings in a mirror: "But angel, can't you see who's in front of you?" The angel could be a friend, a lover, or the narrator's own reflection, and the song never says which. The day after release, a trans woman in Halifax told the sisters it was about her life, and those lines make it easy to see why.

"Angel" sounds like comfort and asks for courage, and it lets you feel loved before you've figured out how to love yourself.

factCheck.claim: Quote: "But if I didn't speak it, it wouldn't be real." (second verse)
factCheck.note: Matches the lyric exactly. It falls in the second verse of the lyric's structure.

factCheck.claim: Klara Söderberg said she was scared of the lyrics and thought they were too direct and a little cheesy
The opening lines describe a life spent afraid and name anxiety, shame and doubt
factCheck.note: The lyric opens with wordless 'ooh' lines. Changed to 'first verse'.

factCheck.claim: Narrator wants to shout at the top of their lungs; the shout stays a wish
factCheck.note: Lyric: 'sometimes I'd like to shout / At the top of my lungs'. The reading is interpretation.

factCheck.claim: Chorus asks for love, compassion and passion, with self-forgiveness in the middle
factCheck.note: Matches 'Give me love and give me compassion / Self-forgiveness and give me some passion'.

factCheck.claim: The chorus repeats with one word changed, 'don't' becoming 'can't'
factCheck.note: The two lines 'don't love me' and 'can't love me' sit back to back within the chorus. The chorus doesn't repeat with a changed word. Rewrote to describe the paired lines.

factCheck.claim: Strummed folk-pop brightness, walking bass line, plain kick-snare-hi-hat beat, relaxed moderate tempo
factCheck.note: Strummed acoustic guitar, walking bass, kick/snare/hi-hat and moderate tempo are agreed by all passes, and 'relaxed' by two. 'Folk-pop' was not agreed, so it was dropped. The draft doesn't claim the strummed part is the one Bengtson added.

factCheck.claim: Two voices are clear and bright; sometimes unison, sometimes one climbs above the melody
factCheck.note: Passes agree on two clear voices with a higher voice above the melody. They disagree on unison versus harmony, so the unison claim was dropped. 'Bright' is supported by two passes.

factCheck.claim: Clean and polished, full without crowding
factCheck.note: All passes agree on clean and polished. Two passes say full but not dense.

factCheck.claim: The duo made it at Bengtson's Studio Rymden in Stockholm for Palomino
factCheck.note: The sources say Palomino was recorded there. The song was later included on the album, so the claim was reworded to be about the album.
